newsitem.title: HONG KONG: China cotton merchandising reform aiding mills.
newsitem.headline: China cotton merchandising reform aiding mills.

text.p: China's cotton industry reforms are giving domestic mills more muscle to pick and choose their purchases, but persistently high cotton stocks mean suppliers now have to compete for customers, traders said on Tuesday.
"Nowadays the domestic mills have more room to bargain with (domestic) suppliers, to select the cotton and to ask them to transfer the cotton to the factory," said one trader.

Hong Kong traders noted that prior to the reforms, in the last quarter of 1996, mills had to pay before receiving the cotton and the purchase price ignored quality, leaving the mills at the mercy of raw cotton suppliers.

While government procurement prices have stayed the same, the system for cotton merchandising has switched to a series of provincial fairs where domestic and international cotton is available to Chinese and joint venture mills, traders said.
The price of cotton at these fairs can fluctuate by four percent above or below the procurement price, traders said.

"The first (fair) was held in November, in Zhengzhou, in Henan province and actual volumes of cotton moved were very small, with people taking a wait-and-see attitude," said one Western industry source.
China's minister in charge of the State Commission for Restructuring the Economy, Li Tieying, said last month that China would use cotton fairs to replace the state-planned system.
Although domestic Chinese cotton prices are dropping as a result, there is still room for imports, traders said.

"The price has dropped to a mill-delivered price of about 83-85 U.S. cents per pound for domestic Chinese cotton, which is a big improvement from over 90 U.S. cents some weeks earlier," said one source.
But the disparity with international cotton prices still exists, traders said, pointing to the New York Cotton Exchange March contract which ended up on Monday at 75.26 cents a pound.
And despite the loosened up domestic market which has led to softer local cotton prices and more accessible supplies for the mills, imports would still continue in 1997, traders said.

"There are many mills in China that would prefer to purchase imported cotton for reasons of consistency and for reasons of more transparent classing and grading for the cotton they purchase," one cotton source said.
China's cotton imports reached 650,000 tonnes in 1996, down by 12.2 percent compared to 1995, customs figures showed.
Demand for cotton yarn and textiles was not expected to pick up significantly this year.

"I don't see much in the way of a pick-up in demand," said one trader, noting that retail markets in Asia, Europe and China were sluggish, while the United States was increasingly opting to source cotton from Latin America.

China's 1997 target output for cotton was projected at 4.25 million tonnes while total demand for cotton was forecast at 5.0 million tonnes, official media reported last month, leaving a potential import gap of 750,000 tonnes in 1997, or an increase of about 15 percent over last year.
